paragraphs.heading: A scientist of weather and ice
paragraphs.text: Alfred Wegener was a German scientist, born in 1880, who worked as a climatologist, geologist, geophysicist, meteorologist and polar researcher. While he lived, people knew him mainly for his meteorology and as a pioneer of polar research. Today he is remembered most for a different idea. In 1912 he suggested that the continents slowly move around the Earth, a proposal known as the continental drift hypothesis.

paragraphs.heading: From astronomy to the atmosphere
paragraphs.text: Wegener studied physics, meteorology and astronomy in Berlin and finished a doctoral dissertation in astronomy in 1905. Even so, he had always kept a strong interest in meteorology and climatology, and his later studies turned to those fields. That same year he became an assistant at an observatory at Lindenberg, where he worked with his brother Kurt, also a scientist interested in meteorology and polar research. The two brothers pioneered the use of weather balloons to follow air masses. In April 1906 they stayed aloft for 52.5 hours on a single balloon flight, a new record for a continuous flight.

paragraphs.heading: First trip to Greenland
paragraphs.text: In 1906 Wegener joined the first of his four expeditions to Greenland. He later looked back on it as a decisive turning point in his life. The expedition, led by the Dane Ludvig Mylius-Erichsen, was sent to study the last unknown part of Greenland's northeastern coast. Near Danmarkshavn, Wegener built the first meteorological station in Greenland and sent up kites and tethered balloons there for meteorological measurements in an Arctic climate. The expedition also brought death close: its leader and two colleagues died on an exploratory trip made with sled dogs.

paragraphs.heading: Proposing that continents move
paragraphs.text: After returning in 1908, Wegener lectured at the University of Marburg on meteorology, applied astronomy and cosmic physics, a post he held until World War I. Students and colleagues there valued how clearly he could explain complex topics and current research without giving up precision. On 6 January 1912 he gave a lecture to the Geological Association at the Senckenberg Museum in Frankfurt am Main. It was his first proposal of continental drift. Later in 1912 he argued for the theory in a long article in three parts and in a shorter summary.

paragraphs.heading: Wintering on the ice
paragraphs.text: Wegener went back to Greenland in 1912–1913 on an expedition of only four men, led by Johan Peter Koch. Before the trip onto the inland ice had even started, a calving glacier almost wiped the expedition out. Koch fell into a glacier crevasse, broke his leg and spent months recovering. Wegener and Koch became the first to spend a winter on the inland ice in northeast Greenland, and inside their hut they drilled down 25 m with an auger. In summer 1913 the four men crossed the inland ice, but ran out of food only a few kilometres from a settlement in western Greenland. Once the last pony and the last dog had been eaten, a clergyman who happened to be visiting a remote congregation picked them up at a fjord.

paragraphs.heading: War, and recognition long after
paragraphs.text: When the First World War began in 1914, Wegener, an infantry reserve officer, was called up at once. He went through fierce fighting on the front in Belgium, but his service there lasted only a few months. After two wounds he was declared unfit for active service and moved to the army weather service. Wegener died in November 1930. Mainstream geology did not accept his drift hypothesis until the 1960s, when discoveries such as palaeomagnetism gave continental drift strong support and, with that, a substantial basis for the present model of plate tectonics.
